An impediment is anything that blocks, slows down, or makes it harder to do something, reach somewhere, or achieve a goal. Think of it as something standing in your way — physically, mentally, legally, or practically.

The key idea is interference. An impediment doesn't have to completely stop you (though it sometimes does). It can simply make your path forward more difficult, slower, or more complicated than it would otherwise be.
The Spectrum: From "Slowing You Down" to "Stopping You Completely"

This is an important nuance. An impediment can sit anywhere on a scale:

  • Mild end: Something that makes a task harder but is manageable. For example, poor lighting is an impediment to reading — it doesn't make reading impossible, but it makes it harder and strains your eyes.
  • Severe end: Something that effectively prevents the action altogether. For example, not having a visa is an impediment to entering a foreign country — in practice, it stops you entirely.

Both uses are correct. The word covers the full range, so pay attention to context when you read it.

1. General, everyday obstacles
This is the broadest use. An impediment here is simply any obstacle or difficulty standing between you and your goal.

  • "Lack of funding is the biggest impediment to the project's success."
  • "Her fear of failure was an impediment to taking risks."
  • "Bad roads are a major impediment to delivering aid to remote villages."

2. Speech impediment (very common phrase)
This is probably the single most common phrase built around this word. A speech impediment is a medical or physical condition that disrupts a person's ability to speak clearly and fluently. Examples include stuttering, lisping, or difficulty pronouncing certain sounds.

  • "He worked with a therapist to manage his speech impediment."
  • "A speech impediment didn't stop her from becoming a great public speaker."

3. Legal impediment
In law, an impediment is a condition or fact that prevents a legal action from being valid. The most classic example is in marriage law — if you are already married to someone else, that is a legal impediment to marrying another person. The new marriage simply cannot legally happen.

  • "The court found no legal impediment to the merger."
  • "Being under the legal age of marriage is an impediment in most countries."

4. Physical impediment
Sometimes used to refer to a physical disability or condition that limits bodily movement or function.

  • "Despite a physical impediment, she competed at the highest level of sport."

"Impediment" is a formal word. In casual conversation, people are more likely to say problem, obstacle, issue, or hurdle. When you see "impediment," the writing or speech is usually in a serious, professional, academic, or legal context — a news article, a business report, a formal speech, or a legal document.

It also carries a slightly cold and clinical tone — it describes the thing getting in the way without a lot of emotional color. It's matter-of-fact.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Obstacle — the most general word. Anything in your way. An impediment is a type of obstacle, but "obstacle" is broader and more casual.
  • Barrier — emphasizes something that separates or keeps apart, like a wall between you and something. A barrier is often harder to get through than a general impediment.
  • Hindrance — very close to impediment. A hindrance also means something making things harder. The two are nearly interchangeable, but "impediment" is slightly more formal and is more often used in legal or medical contexts.
  • Hurdle — implies something you can get over, with effort. It has a more optimistic tone than "impediment."
  • Obstruction — suggests something more deliberately or physically blocking the way, often used in physical or legal contexts (like obstruction of justice).
Common Phrases and Patterns to Remember

• an impediment to something — this is the standard structure. You always say an impediment to a goal, action, or process: "an impediment to peace," "an impediment to learning," "an impediment to progress."
  • without impediment — meaning freely, without anything getting in the way. "The goods passed through customs without impediment."
  • remove/clear an impediment — to get rid of the obstacle. "They worked hard to remove the impediments to a fair trial."
  • speech impediment — a fixed phrase used in medical and everyday contexts.
  • legal impediment — a fixed phrase used in law.

• "Poverty is a serious impediment to educational achievement."
  • "The new law removes a key impediment to starting a small business."
  • "His lack of confidence was the only impediment standing between him and success."
  • "The speech impediment she had as a child no longer affects her today."
  • "There is no legal impediment to the two companies merging."
  • "Heavy snow was an impediment to travel across the entire region."

An impediment is anything — a condition, a fact, a physical thing, or a circumstance — that makes it harder or impossible to do, reach, or achieve something. It stands in the way of progress or action, whether mildly or completely.
